title: 2.5.7 Plain English to Pseudocode: try/catch
description: Turn plain-English steps into pseudocode for try/catch: attempt a risky step, run the catch only if it fails, then carry on either way.
sourceRef: designed: practice for Definition 2.5.2 (try...catch control flow)

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English:

**1.** **Try** to print `quantity`. (This line is risky: `quantity` was never created, so it will fail.)

**2.** If that failed, **catch** it: print `Could not read quantity.` If it did not fail, skip this step.

**3.** After the try/catch, whichever way it went, print `Done.`

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you read it: there is no `if` in the code, but the diamond "did that line fail?" is the question `try` asks for you, and **both** exits reach the last print.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Number every line, including indented ones. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `TRY` (attempt the risky steps, indented under it)
- `CATCH` (runs only if a step in the TRY failed, steps indented under it) and `END TRY`
- `PRINT total` (show something)

Plain English is fine ("if that fails, ..."). Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, trace it twice by hand: once when the try fails and once when it works. `Done.` should print both times, and the catch message only when it failed.
hints: The catch step belongs to the failure answer: it does not run when the try worked.
"Done." is after END TRY, so it runs whichever path was taken.

requirements.title: Numbered steps
requirements.description: Number your steps 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: Write at least four lines that start with a number, each with a step written after it.

requirements.title: The risky line is tried first
requirements.description: A TRY step that attempts to print quantity.
requirements.hint: Start with a TRY step that prints quantity.

requirements.title: There is a catch for failure
requirements.description: A catch step that only applies when the try failed.
requirements.hint: Add a CATCH step: what happens if the try fails.

requirements.title: The message is in the catch
requirements.description: Could not read quantity. is printed in the catch (failure) part, after the catch begins.
requirements.hint: Put the Could not read quantity. message under CATCH.

requirements.title: Done runs either way
requirements.description: Done. is printed after the try/catch has finished, so both paths reach it.
requirements.hint: Move Done. to after END TRY so both paths reach it.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The program is: try { console.log(quantity); } catch (err) { console.log("Could not read quantity."); } console.log("Done."). quantity was never created, so the try fails. The point: the catch runs ONLY when the try fails; the "Done." line is after the whole try/catch so it runs on both paths. Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, ELSE, END IF, FOR EACH, END FOR, CALL, PRINT, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite (for example the Done print inside the catch only, or the Could not read message printed outside the catch). Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: Numbered steps
rubric.description: The student numbered their steps (1. 2. 3. or similar), at least four of them.

rubric.title: The risky line is tried first
rubric.description: The steps must say the print of quantity is TRIED or ATTEMPTED (a TRY step, or "try to print quantity"), before any failure handling. If print quantity is just an ordinary step with no TRY or attempt wording anywhere, this is NOT met, even when a CATCH step follows.

rubric.title: There is a catch for failure
rubric.description: There is a CATCH (or "if that fails / on error") step that applies only when the try failed.

rubric.title: The message is in the catch
rubric.description: The message "Could not read quantity." is printed INSIDE the catch part, so it runs only when the try failed. A message printed every time, or before the catch, does not meet this.

rubric.title: Done runs either way
rubric.description: "Done." is printed AFTER the try/catch has finished (after END TRY), so it runs whether or not the try failed. Printing it only inside the catch does not meet this.
